<reason>A high-skill debate decided by whose reading of "same basic terms" survives. B's parity reading (one framework, equal standing, hazard-appropriate controls) fits the motion's actual wording: "basic" and "once safety standards are met" absorb A's central evidence, since the pre-market gate A kept citing is the motion's own stated condition, not a breach of it. B also answered A's vacuity pressure directly by naming concrete violations (name bans, warning labels, procurement exclusion), and repeatedly exposed A's inconsistency in calling production-method disclosure "ordinary practice" defensively while treating it as regime-defining offensively. A's dilemma construction was genuinely clever and its rebuttals caught real drift in B's definitions, but A's closing inversion conceded the substantive policy is identical, leaving A asking for negation on a strict semantics of "same" that the word "basic" undercuts. B's "your regime is the motion with the paperwork shown" convergence was the cleaner, more decisive frame.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The vacuity exchange: A's Q1 demanded B name one requirement short of a ban that would violate the motion, and B's A1 directly named three (forbidding the word "chicken," warning-style labels, procurement exclusion), defusing A's "contentless motion" win condition; paired with B4.4's "They named a hazard. A hazard is not a regime," this blunted A's strongest line. A's best counter was A2.1-A2.4 catching B's definitional expansion and the closing observation that B walked past cell-line authentication and medium approval, but those hits only kept it competitive.</best_rebuttal>
